title: Average Value
body:
[[Mean]]
[[Median]]
[[Mode]]

---

The three measures of **central tendency**: one number standing in for a whole dataset. All three
answer "where is this data?", and they disagree exactly when the data is skewed, which is why the
course teaches three instead of one.

| Measure | Definition | Uses every value? | Survives outliers? | Works on categories? |
|---|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| [[Mean]] | $\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum x_i$ | yes | no | no |
| [[Median]] | middle value once sorted | no | yes | no |
| [[Mode]] | most frequent value | no | yes | yes |

**Which one is right is a question about the data, not about preference.** Symmetric and clean
wants the [[Mean]], because it uses all the information and it is what every later formula in
[[STATISTICS]] is built from. Skewed or outlier-prone wants the [[Median]]: incomes, house prices,
response times. Qualitative data leaves you only the [[Mode]], since you cannot average colours.

On a symmetric distribution all three land on the same value. On a right-skewed one they separate
in order, $\text{mode} < \text{median} < \text{mean}$, because only the mean feels the tail. That
ordering is the fastest way to detect skew from a summary table with no plot attached.

> [!note] Not to be confused with the calculus sense
> The **average value of a function** over $[a,b]$, $\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$, is a
> different object with the same name and it belongs to [[CALCULUS 1]] and [[CALCULUS 2]]. The two
> do connect: the continuous case is the discrete average with the sum replaced by an
> [[Integral]], and $E[X] = \int x f(x)\,dx$ in [[Random Variable]] is precisely that move applied
> to a density. But this note is the statistics one, and it is an index into the three sample
> measures above.

## Related

- [[Variance]]: the other half of a summary. A centre with no spread reported is not a summary
- [[Random Variable]]: expected value is the [[Mean]] promoted from a dataset to a distribution
